findings.exact_text: Arda swung free on the cut length still gripped in his fist, and Nisa—reading the exact same moment he did—leaned back and hauled, and his hand found her wrist
findings.reason: After cutting the line, Nisa is across the gap holding the line, so her wrist being reachable by his hand is physically unclear; the rescue mechanics are incoherent.

findings.exact_text: There was no time to unlash.
findings.reason: Cutting the line is justified, but the line was anchored to the trunk, not to him; why he must cut to free himself is unclear.

findings.exact_text: The glider still held where the old knot-trunk leaned.
findings.reason: The line was unfastened and carried inland, so the glider is no longer secured; also two gliders existed but Nisa's glider is never accounted for.

findings.exact_text: the proof was lashed to his harness
findings.reason: Journal and tag were held or carried by hand; lashing is never shown. Also S199 has the tag in his palm, a minor inconsistency.

findings.exact_text: Somewhere ahead the cloud wall was, certainly, closing.
findings.reason: Cloud wall was described as on the far side of the corridor beyond the island, yet the corridor and the wall are placed oddly relative to the island, and the bridge route to the camp is inconsistent.

findings.exact_text: found the great root span torn loose in the wind
findings.reason: The bridge Arda crossed was a different, sagging one; the camp is reached without clear crossing, so the return route geography is confusing.

findings.exact_text: the last light
findings.reason: They land in last light, yet the sunset appears afterward and the corridor light was dying earlier; time-of-day is inconsistent.

findings.exact_text: what, on that vanished island, waited behind the stone gate for someone to come back and finish the story.
findings.reason: Ending lands on a hook but dilutes the spine's required ending of the island dissolving with Arda holding the tag; minor.

findings.exact_text: decades old at least.
findings.reason: Asserts a specific age for the earlier expedition, a durable canon claim not supported by authority.

findings.exact_text: The bridge made it to them—or rather, didn't.
findings.reason: Awkward, confusing phrasing.

findings.exact_text: known sky opening ahead like a held breath let go
findings.reason: Muddled simile.

findings.exact_text: Nisa followed him in despite everything
findings.reason: Spine has Arda reaching the camp first; text has them arrive together, and Nisa's ridge split-up is shortened.

findings.exact_text: Someone should look at the sky while you chase knots.
findings.reason: Nisa leaves for a ridge ten minutes, yet returns running with a corridor report; the split and reunion are compressed and unclear.

findings.exact_text: arriving at his shoulder
findings.reason: This compressed body-position phrase is unnatural; English ordinarily places someone “at his side” or “beside him.”

findings.exact_text: something she wished she didn't want
findings.reason: The nested verbs create an unclear, unnatural expression of reluctant agreement.

findings.exact_text: a slope of tangle
findings.reason: “Tangle” is not naturally used as a mass noun in this construction; “a tangled slope” conveys the image clearly.

findings.exact_text: flattened every tree inland into a lean
findings.reason: “Into a lean” is an unnatural result phrase for trees bent persistently by wind.

findings.exact_text: Around the trunk, half-sunk into bark that had grown over it, ran a length
findings.reason: The extended inverted construction delays the subject and makes the physical image unnecessarily difficult to parse.

findings.exact_text: dropped away to cloud sea
findings.reason: The established geographical noun phrase requires the article: “the cloud sea.”

findings.exact_text: a cliff overlook gave him the whole interior at a glance
findings.reason: “Cliff overlook” and “gave him the whole interior” form strained collocations that obscure the otherwise simple viewpoint description.

findings.exact_text: the same corridor we arrived
findings.reason: “Arrived” cannot directly take “corridor” as its object; the sentence needs a preposition such as “through.”

findings.exact_text: half-hidden by fern
findings.reason: For ordinary visible vegetation, English naturally uses “ferns” or “a fern,” not singular bare “fern.”

findings.exact_text: reading the exact same moment he did
findings.reason: A person can read a situation or intention, but “read a moment” is an unnatural and unclear collocation here.

findings.exact_text: the old knot-trunk
findings.reason: The improvised compound “knot-trunk” is unnecessarily compressed and briefly ambiguous.

findings.exact_text: laughed until she had to stop
findings.reason: This is tautological and vague; specifying that she ran out of breath gives the phrase a natural endpoint.

target_segments.source_text: "I saw it first," Nisa said, arriving at his shoulder.
Then at him, and her jaw set in the particular way it did when she was about to agree with something she wished she didn't want.
It was a slope of tangle—a hillside of old roots spilled over the island's edge like the fingers of something buried.
Wind had flattened every tree inland into a lean, as if the whole forest had spent centuries flinching from one direction.
Around the trunk, half-sunk into bark that had grown over it, ran a length of bleached rope fiber, knotted in a hitch he almost recognized—a guild-style anchor, but not any pattern currently taught.
Bridges made of living root spanned gaps that dropped away to cloud sea, grown in arcs no carpenter could copy.
Somewhere behind them the corridor they'd flown through was, presumably, still open.
Somewhere ahead the cloud wall was, certainly, closing.
Someone should look at the sky while you chase knots." She was already climbing.
On the far side of the bridge, a cliff overlook gave him the whole interior at a glance, and what he saw stopped him cold: the old knots didn't stop.
The bones of an expedition, decades old at least.
Nisa followed him in despite everything, because whatever she thought of him right now, she wasn't going to let him search it alone.
Then the final pages: *We depart by the same corridor we arrived.
At the camp's far edge, half-hidden by fern, a carved wind-vane pointed deeper inland—and beyond it, visible through a break in the trees, a shape on the high ground.
The bridge made it to them—or rather, didn't.

They came down through the mist-filled trees at a dead run and found the great root span torn loose in the wind, its far anchor ripped out, the whole thing sagging and thrashing above a drop into the cloud sea.
There was no time to unlash.
There was only one thing left to do, and he did it with his knife and hated every centimeter of it: he cut the line.

The bridge fell away beneath him into the cloud sea, taking the rope's last anchor with it, and Arda swung free on the cut length still gripped in his fist, and Nisa—reading the exact same moment he did—leaned back and hauled, and his hand found her wrist, and her grip found him, and that was what saved him.
The glider still held where the old knot-trunk leaned.

The corridor closed behind them the way a door closes—steadily, without malice—and they came through the last open stretch with the cloud wall breathing on their wings and known sky opening ahead like a held breath let go.
He knew only that it had been real, and that the proof was lashed to his harness.
They landed at Stormbreak Watch in the last light, shaking, mud-caked, out of rope, and entirely, completely victorious.
Nisa sat down on the wooden rail and laughed until she had to stop.

Then he took out the glider-tag and held it in his open palm, turning it so the unknown name caught the sunset, and wondered who had tied those knots, and whether they had ever made it home—and what, on that vanished island, waited behind the stone gate for someone to come back and finish the story.
